title: AI Agents: AI That Does Things
hook: A chatbot answers; an agent acts. The new frontier is AI that can browse, click, book, and complete multi-step tasks for you — powerful, and exactly why you keep it on a leash.
key_points: An agent doesn't just reply — it takes actions: searching, filling forms, using apps.
It chains steps together to finish a goal, not just answer one question.
More power means more risk: a wrong step now does something, not just says something.
Keep a human in the loop and limit what an agent is allowed to touch.
content_html: For its first couple of years, mainstream AI mostly talked: you asked, it answered, and what you did with the answer was up to you. The big shift now underway is toward agents — AI that doesn't just respond but acts. Instead of telling you how to book a flight, an agent can open a browser, search the options, fill in the form, and complete the booking. It breaks a goal into steps, takes each one, checks the result, and keeps going until the task is done.
extra_html: This is genuinely powerful, and it's where a lot of the industry is heading: assistants that handle errands, manage your calendar, do research and produce a finished document, or operate software on your behalf. But notice what changes when AI can act rather than just speak — the stakes of its mistakes go up sharply. A hallucination in a chatbot wastes a minute; a wrong move by an agent might send the wrong email, buy the wrong thing, or delete a file. Agents can also be tricked into harmful actions through manipulated content they encounter while working. So the safety mindset matters more, not less: keep a human in the loop to approve consequential steps, limit what an agent is allowed to access (your money, your accounts, your files), and start with low-stakes tasks. Agents are likely the next big leap in everyday AI — useful to understand now, and to adopt with your eyes open.

related.title: Chatbots & Assistants
related.hook: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini feel like talking to a person, but they're generative AI with a chat wrapper — brilliant writing partners, unreliable encyclopedias.

related.title: AI at Work
related.hook: The biggest everyday payoff from AI is at work: drafting the email, summarizing the meeting, untangling the spreadsheet formula. The trick is using it without leaking secrets or trust.

related.title: Over-Relying on AI
related.hook: The subtle risk isn't that AI fails — it's that it usually works, so you stop checking. Trusting a confident machine over your own judgment is its own kind of mistake.

related.title: Hackers Talked Meta's AI Into Handing Over Accounts
related.hook: Attackers stole Instagram accounts not by cracking passwords, but by asking Meta's support AI to relink them — proof that an AI agent with real permissions can be talked into real harm.

related.title: What If Millions of AI Agents Start Talking to Each Other?
related.hook: Google DeepMind is funding research into a problem barely here yet: not one AI agent misbehaving, but millions of them interacting online with no human watching.

flashcards.prompt: What's the difference between a chatbot and an AI agent?

choices.text: A chatbot answers; an agent takes actions to complete a task
Nothing — they're two words for the same thing
An agent is just a faster chatbot

flashcards.explanation_html: An agent goes beyond replying: it can browse, click, fill forms, and chain multiple steps to actually get something done on your behalf.

flashcards.prompt: Why do AI agents need tighter guardrails than chatbots?
flashcards.back_html: Because a mistake now does something in the real world — books, buys, sends — instead of just printing wrong text. Keep a human approving key steps.
